expectedText:
COMMISSIONED EMPLOYEE ("INSIDE SALES") OVERTIME EXEMPTION (WAGE ORDERS 4 AND 7, § 3(D); PEABODY V. TIME WARNER CABLE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the "commissioned employee" overtime exemption — the provision of Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Orders 4-2001 and 7-2001 under which the daily and weekly overtime rules do not apply to an employee, such as Jordan Lee, whose earnings exceed one and one-half times the minimum wage if more than half of that employee's compensation represents commissions. This document describes the overtime default the exemption modifies, the text and coverage of the wage-order provision, the exemption's two prongs and who bears the burden of proving them, the minimum-wage figure the earnings prong is measured against, the California Supreme Court's decision in Peabody v. Time Warner Cable on which pay period a commission counts toward, the case law defining what is and is not a "commission," the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published enforcement positions, and the obligations the exemption leaves untouched. It describes the law; it does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, and it does not create, modify, or interpret any commission plan.

THE OVERTIME DEFAULT AND WHY THIS EXEMPTION LIVES IN THE WAGE ORDERS
California's overtime statute, Labor Code section 510(a), provides that work in excess of eight hours in one workday, work in excess of 40 hours in a workweek, and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in a workweek are compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay, with work beyond 12 hours in a day (and beyond eight hours on a seventh day) compensated at no less than twice the regular rate. The commissioned employee exemption is not stated in that statute or anywhere else in the Labor Code. It appears in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission. Labor Code section 515(b) supplies the statutory footing: it provides that, except as otherwise provided in that section and in section 511(g), nothing in section 515 requires the Commission to alter an exemption from provisions regulating hours of work that was contained in a valid wage order in effect in 1997, and that the Commission may review, retain, or eliminate such an exemption. The commissioned employee exemption predates 1997 — the Court of Appeal in Keyes Motors, Inc. v. Division of Labor Standards Enforcement construed the version in Wage Order 7-80 in 1987 — and was retained in the 2001 wage orders.

The statement that the exemption "predates 1997" rests on the Keyes Motors opinion's 1987 construction of the corresponding subsection of Wage Order 7-80; this document did not fetch the pre-2001 wage orders themselves or the Commission's statements of basis for the 2001 orders.

THE TEXT OF SECTION 3(D) AND WHICH WAGE ORDERS CONTAIN IT
Section 3(D) of Wage Order 4-2001 (professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations) provides that the overtime provisions of subsections 3(A), (B), and (C) do not apply to any employee whose earnings exceed one and one-half times the minimum wage if more than half of that employee's compensation represents commissions. Section 3(D) of Wage Order 7-2001 (the mercantile industry) contains the same provision in the same words. The exemption is specific to those two wage orders. The California Supreme Court in Peabody v. Time Warner Cable noted that Wage Order 4 "covers salespersons and sales agents," and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Manual describes the exemption as one for "[c]ertain commissioned salespersons covered either by Order 4-2001 or 7-2001." By contrast, the Court of Appeal in Keyes Motors observed that the transportation-industry wage order (Order 9), which applied to mechanics at independent repair shops, contained no overtime exemption for employees earning commissions. Which wage order governs a given employee therefore determines whether the exemption is available at all.

TWO PRONGS, NARROW CONSTRUCTION, AND THE EMPLOYER'S BURDEN OF PROOF
Section 3(D) has two conditions, and both must be met: (1) a minimum-earnings prong — the employee's earnings must exceed one and one-half times the minimum wage — and (2) a commission-proportion prong — more than half of the employee's compensation must represent commissions. The California Supreme Court in Peabody v. Time Warner Cable referred to these as the exemption's "minimum earnings prong" and "second prong." Two general principles govern how the conditions are read. First, because statutes governing conditions of employment are construed broadly in favor of protecting employees, exemptions from the overtime requirements are narrowly construed against the employer, and their application is limited to employees plainly and unmistakably within their terms (Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co.; Peabody). Second, the assertion of an overtime exemption is an affirmative defense, so the employer bears the burden of proving that the employee is exempt (Ramirez). In Peabody the court expressly declined to decide whether the second prong was met on the facts before it, resolving the case on the minimum-earnings prong alone.

Neither Ramirez nor Peabody defines the measuring period for the "more than half" prong; the DLSE's enforcement position on that point is described in a later clause.

THE MINIMUM-EARNINGS PRONG AND THE MINIMUM WAGE IT IS MEASURED AGAINST
The first prong requires that the employee's earnings "exceed" one and one-half times the minimum wage. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states that, effective January 1, 2026, the California minimum wage is $16.90 per hour for all employers not otherwise covered by a higher industry-specific or local minimum wage; one and one-half times that figure is $25.35 per hour, so an employee's earnings must exceed $25.35 for each hour worked for this prong to be met at the statewide rate. The statewide minimum wage adjusts annually: Labor Code section 1182.12(c)(1) directs the Director of Finance, on or before each August 1, to calculate an adjusted minimum wage that increases the rate by the lesser of 3.5 percent and the change in the national CPI-W, rounded to the nearest ten cents, taking effect the following January 1. Because the earnings threshold is tied to the minimum wage, it rises each time the minimum wage does. Peabody illustrated the arithmetic under the then-applicable $8.00 minimum wage: an employee working 45 hours in a week could satisfy the prong only if paid more than $540 for that week ($12 times 45 hours).

PEABODY V. TIME WARNER CABLE: THE EARNINGS PRONG IS MEASURED BY WHAT IS ACTUALLY PAID IN EACH PAY PERIOD
In Peabody v. Time Warner Cable, Inc. (2014) 59 Cal.4th 662, the California Supreme Court answered a question certified by the Ninth Circuit: whether an employer may attribute commission wages paid in one pay period to other pay periods in order to satisfy California's compensation requirements. The employee received biweekly paychecks of $769.23 in hourly wages (about $9.61 per hour on a 40-hour week) and commission wages roughly every other pay period; most of her paychecks were therefore below one and one-half times the minimum wage. The employer argued that commissions paid at month's end should be reassigned to the weeks of the preceding month in which they were earned. The court held that whether the minimum-earnings prong is satisfied depends on the amount of wages actually paid in a pay period, and that an employer may not attribute wages paid in one pay period to a prior pay period to cure a shortfall. The court reasoned that Labor Code section 204(a) requires all earned wages, including commissions, to be paid at least semimonthly; that Labor Code section 200(a) defines "wages" to include amounts calculated on a commission basis; that requiring the minimum amount to be paid in each pay period mitigates the burden of exempting the employee from overtime; and that reassigning wages would be inconsistent with the semimonthly-pay and itemized-wage-statement statutes. At the same time, the court made clear that there is no obligation to pay unearned commissions in any pay period — commissions are owed only when earned, even if that occurs monthly, quarterly, or less often. The court also declined to follow the federal counterpart exemption, 29 U.S.C. § 207(i), because federal law neither requires semimonthly pay nor forbids deferring earned commissions.

  Known gap: Peabody decided only the minimum-earnings prong; it did not decide whether the employee's commissions were more than half of her compensation (see footnote 4) and did not address the definition of "commission." Its holding is framed around the semimonthly pay periods required by Labor Code section 204(a); the opinion notes that different statutory pay-period rules exist for certain executive, administrative, and professional employees and for commissioned vehicle salespersons under section 204.1, and this document does not analyze how the holding applies under those alternative pay-period rules. The court's footnote 7 extends the same no-reassignment reasoning to the minimum wage; that footnote is quoted in a later clause. The 29 U.S.C. § 207(i) federal exemption was not fetched for this document and is described only as Peabody characterized it.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "COMMISSION": LABOR CODE SECTION 204.1 AND THE KEYES MOTORS TWO-PART TEST
The wage orders do not define "commission." The courts have borrowed the definition in Labor Code section 204.1, which — although the section itself addresses the pay-timing of vehicle dealers' employees — defines commission wages as compensation paid to any person for services rendered in the sale of the employer's property or services and based proportionately upon the amount or value thereof. In Keyes Motors, Inc. v. Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (1987) 197 Cal.App.3d 557, the Court of Appeal read section 204.1 as setting up two requirements, both of which must be met: first, the employees must be involved principally in selling a product or service, not making the product or rendering the service; second, the amount of their compensation must be a percent of the price of the product or service. Applying that test, the court held that automobile mechanics paid a percentage of the hourly rate charged to customers were not commissioned employees because a mechanic performs labor, not sales. In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785, the California Supreme Court agreed that section 204.1's definition is generally applicable and adopted the Keyes Motors formulation, remanding for a determination whether a bottled-water route salesman was principally engaged in selling. Later Courts of Appeal have read the second requirement according to the statute's "amount or value" language rather than as a rigid percentage-of-price rule: Areso v. CarMax, Inc. (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 996 held that a uniform payment for each vehicle sold is commission compensation because it is based proportionately on the amount (number) of vehicles sold, and Muldrow v. Surrex Solutions Corp. (2012) 208 Cal.App.4th 1381 held that recruiters paid a percentage of the "adjusted gross profit" on placements, a figure derived from the billing rate less costs, received commissions, rejecting the argument that a commission must be based strictly and solely on a percentage of price. By contrast, as Areso recounts, Harris v. Investor's Business Daily, Inc. (2006) 138 Cal.App.4th 28 held that telemarketers paid under a point system not tied to the price of the subscriptions they sold were not paid commissions.

Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11070, subd. 3(D)) should be interpreted to include only those commissions that are based strictly, and solely, on a percentage of the price of the product or service rendered constitutes an excessively narrow and wooden application of Keyes Motors and Ramirez"
  — Muldrow v. Surrex Solutions Corp. (2012) 208 Cal.App.4th 1381 (CourtListener text), 208 Cal.App.4th 1381, 1395 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811300/muldrow-v-surrex-solutions-corp/)
  Known gap: Harris v. Investor's Business Daily was not fetched for this document; it is described only as the Areso opinion characterized it, and is not cited as a source. Whether a particular employee is "involved principally in selling" is a fact question that Ramirez remanded for trial rather than resolved; Muldrow found the requirement met on evidence that the recruiters' search, screening, and cold-calling activities were prerequisites to accomplishing a sale. Labor Code section 2751(c), which incorporates the section 204.1 definition for the written-commission-contract requirement, also excludes short-term productivity bonuses, temporary variable incentive payments, and bonus and profit-sharing plans from "commission" for that section's purposes only; that exclusion is stated for section 2751 and no source fetched for this document applies it to the wage-order exemption. The DLSE Enforcement Manual's distinction between commissions and piece-rate pay (§ 2.5.4, as quoted in Areso) was not separately fetched and is not relied on here.

THE DLSE'S PUBLISHED ENFORCEMENT POSITIONS: WORKWEEK-BY-WORKWEEK COMPLIANCE, DRAWS, THE REPRESENTATIVE PERIOD, AND RECORDS
The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, section 50.6, sets out the agency's positions on the exemption. Section 50.6.1 states that, for each workweek in the pay period, the employee's earnings — whether actual commissions or a guaranteed draw for the workweek against commissions to be earned within that workweek — must exceed 1.5 times the minimum wage for each hour worked; that this payment must be made in each pay period, so that it is not permissible to defer any part of the wages due for one period until payment of the wages for a later period; that compliance is determined on a workweek basis; and that the second component (more than half of earnings from commissions) must also be satisfied in each workweek, with overtime due for any week in which it is not met, although the agency will defer the actual determination until the reconciliation date after the second pay period. The California Supreme Court in Peabody quoted the first three of these points and adopted the agency's interpretation after independently determining that it was correct. The Manual further states that a guaranteed draw counts toward the earnings prong only if it can be recovered from commissions earned in that same workweek and not from future workweeks; that whether commissions constitute most of the employee's pay is tested over a "representative period" of not less than one month; that the employer bears the responsibility of proving the exemption and must keep records clearly indicating the amount and nature of payments, including a copy or summary of the commission agreement and the applicable representative period; and that consistent commission earnings below, at, or near the draw are indicative of a commission plan that is not bona fide.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "1. By its terms, section 3(D) removes only the overtime provisions of subsections 3(A), (B), and (C). It does not exempt the employee from the wage orders' other requirements. In particular, section 4(B) of Wage Order 4-2001 requires every employer to pay each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise — and Peabody's footnote 7 applied the same no-reassignment rule to the minimum wage, observing that the answer is, if anything, clearer in that context. Separately, Labor Code section 2751 requires that whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment for services to be rendered within California and the contemplated method of payment involves commissions, the contract must be in writing and set forth the method by which the commissions are computed and paid; the employer must give the employee a signed copy and obtain a signed receipt. Finally, Wage Orders 4 and 7 each provide that sections 3 through 12 do not apply at all to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities as defined in those orders; the commissioned employee exemption operates within section 3 for employees who are otherwise covered by it.

expectedJSON.body: Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the "commissioned employee" overtime exemption — the provision of Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Orders 4-2001 and 7-2001 under which the daily and weekly overtime rules do not apply to an employee, such as Jordan Lee, whose earnings exceed one and one-half times the minimum wage if more than half of that employee's compensation represents commissions. This document describes the overtime default the exemption modifies, the text and coverage of the wage-order provision, the exemption's two prongs and who bears the burden of proving them, the minimum-wage figure the earnings prong is measured against, the California Supreme Court's decision in Peabody v. Time Warner Cable on which pay period a commission counts toward, the case law defining what is and is not a "commission," the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published enforcement positions, and the obligations the exemption leaves untouched. It describes the law; it does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, and it does not create, modify, or interpret any commission plan.

California's overtime statute, Labor Code section 510(a), provides that work in excess of eight hours in one workday, work in excess of 40 hours in a workweek, and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in a workweek are compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay, with work beyond 12 hours in a day (and beyond eight hours on a seventh day) compensated at no less than twice the regular rate. The commissioned employee exemption is not stated in that statute or anywhere else in the Labor Code. It appears in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission. Labor Code section 515(b) supplies the statutory footing: it provides that, except as otherwise provided in that section and in section 511(g), nothing in section 515 requires the Commission to alter an exemption from provisions regulating hours of work that was contained in a valid wage order in effect in 1997, and that the Commission may review, retain, or eliminate such an exemption. The commissioned employee exemption predates 1997 — the Court of Appeal in Keyes Motors, Inc. v. Division of Labor Standards Enforcement construed the version in Wage Order 7-80 in 1987 — and was retained in the 2001 wage orders.

Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee.

Section 3(D) of Wage Order 7-2001 (the mercantile industry) contains the same provision in the same words. The exemption is specific to those two wage orders. The California Supreme Court in Peabody v. Time Warner Cable noted that Wage Order 4 "covers salespersons and sales agents," and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Manual describes the exemption as one for "[c]ertain commissioned salespersons covered either by Order 4-2001 or 7-2001." By contrast, the Court of Appeal in Keyes Motors observed that the transportation-industry wage order (Order 9), which applied to mechanics at independent repair shops, contained no overtime exemption for employees earning commissions. Which wage order governs a given employee therefore determines whether the exemption is available at all.

expectedJSON.body: Section 3(D) has two conditions, and both must be met: (1) a minimum-earnings prong — the employee's earnings must exceed one and one-half times the minimum wage — and (2) a commission-proportion prong — more than half of the employee's compensation must represent commissions. The California Supreme Court in Peabody v. Time Warner Cable referred to these as the exemption's "minimum earnings prong" and "second prong." Two general principles govern how the conditions are read. First, because statutes governing conditions of employment are construed broadly in favor of protecting employees, exemptions from the overtime requirements are narrowly construed against the employer, and their application is limited to employees plainly and unmistakably within their terms (Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co.; Peabody). Second, the assertion of an overtime exemption is an affirmative defense, so the employer bears the burden of proving that the employee is exempt (Ramirez). In Peabody the court expressly declined to decide whether the second prong was met on the facts before it, resolving the case on the minimum-earnings prong alone.

expectedJSON.body: The first prong requires that the employee's earnings "exceed" one and one-half times the minimum wage. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states that, effective January 1, 2026, the California minimum wage is $16.90 per hour for all employers not otherwise covered by a higher industry-specific or local minimum wage; one and one-half times that figure is $25.35 per hour, so an employee's earnings must exceed $25.35 for each hour worked for this prong to be met at the statewide rate. The statewide minimum wage adjusts annually: Labor Code section 1182.12(c)(1) directs the Director of Finance, on or before each August 1, to calculate an adjusted minimum wage that increases the rate by the lesser of 3.5 percent and the change in the national CPI-W, rounded to the nearest ten cents, taking effect the following January 1. Because the earnings threshold is tied to the minimum wage, it rises each time the minimum wage does. Peabody illustrated the arithmetic under the then-applicable $8.00 minimum wage: an employee working 45 hours in a week could satisfy the prong only if paid more than $540 for that week ($12 times 45 hours).

expectedJSON.body: In Peabody v. Time Warner Cable, Inc. (2014) 59 Cal.4th 662, the California Supreme Court answered a question certified by the Ninth Circuit: whether an employer may attribute commission wages paid in one pay period to other pay periods in order to satisfy California's compensation requirements. The employee received biweekly paychecks of $769.23 in hourly wages (about $9.61 per hour on a 40-hour week) and commission wages roughly every other pay period; most of her paychecks were therefore below one and one-half times the minimum wage. The employer argued that commissions paid at month's end should be reassigned to the weeks of the preceding month in which they were earned. The court held that whether the minimum-earnings prong is satisfied depends on the amount of wages actually paid in a pay period, and that an employer may not attribute wages paid in one pay period to a prior pay period to cure a shortfall. The court reasoned that Labor Code section 204(a) requires all earned wages, including commissions, to be paid at least semimonthly; that Labor Code section 200(a) defines "wages" to include amounts calculated on a commission basis; that requiring the minimum amount to be paid in each pay period mitigates the burden of exempting the employee from overtime; and that reassigning wages would be inconsistent with the semimonthly-pay and itemized-wage-statement statutes. At the same time, the court made clear that there is no obligation to pay unearned commissions in any pay period — commissions are owed only when earned, even if that occurs monthly, quarterly, or less often. The court also declined to follow the federal counterpart exemption, 29 U.S.C. § 207(i), because federal law neither requires semimonthly pay nor forbids deferring earned commissions.

expectedJSON.body: The wage orders do not define "commission." The courts have borrowed the definition in Labor Code section 204.1, which — although the section itself addresses the pay-timing of vehicle dealers' employees — defines commission wages as compensation paid to any person for services rendered in the sale of the employer's property or services and based proportionately upon the amount or value thereof. In Keyes Motors, Inc. v. Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (1987) 197 Cal.App.3d 557, the Court of Appeal read section 204.1 as setting up two requirements, both of which must be met: first, the employees must be involved principally in selling a product or service, not making the product or rendering the service; second, the amount of their compensation must be a percent of the price of the product or service. Applying that test, the court held that automobile mechanics paid a percentage of the hourly rate charged to customers were not commissioned employees because a mechanic performs labor, not sales. In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785, the California Supreme Court agreed that section 204.1's definition is generally applicable and adopted the Keyes Motors formulation, remanding for a determination whether a bottled-water route salesman was principally engaged in selling. Later Courts of Appeal have read the second requirement according to the statute's "amount or value" language rather than as a rigid percentage-of-price rule: Areso v. CarMax, Inc. (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 996 held that a uniform payment for each vehicle sold is commission compensation because it is based proportionately on the amount (number) of vehicles sold, and Muldrow v. Surrex Solutions Corp. (2012) 208 Cal.App.4th 1381 held that recruiters paid a percentage of the "adjusted gross profit" on placements, a figure derived from the billing rate less costs, received commissions, rejecting the argument that a commission must be based strictly and solely on a percentage of price. By contrast, as Areso recounts, Harris v. Investor's Business Daily, Inc. (2006) 138 Cal.App.4th 28 held that telemarketers paid under a point system not tied to the price of the subscriptions they sold were not paid commissions.

Second, the amount of their compensation must be a percent of the price of the product or service. Mechanics are engaged in rendering a service, not selling it.

expectedJSON.gap: Harris v. Investor's Business Daily was not fetched for this document; it is described only as the Areso opinion characterized it, and is not cited as a source. Whether a particular employee is "involved principally in selling" is a fact question that Ramirez remanded for trial rather than resolved; Muldrow found the requirement met on evidence that the recruiters' search, screening, and cold-calling activities were prerequisites to accomplishing a sale. Labor Code section 2751(c), which incorporates the section 204.1 definition for the written-commission-contract requirement, also excludes short-term productivity bonuses, temporary variable incentive payments, and bonus and profit-sharing plans from "commission" for that section's purposes only; that exclusion is stated for section 2751 and no source fetched for this document applies it to the wage-order exemption. The DLSE Enforcement Manual's distinction between commissions and piece-rate pay (§ 2.5.4, as quoted in Areso) was not separately fetched and is not relied on here.

expectedJSON.body: The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, section 50.6, sets out the agency's positions on the exemption. Section 50.6.1 states that, for each workweek in the pay period, the employee's earnings — whether actual commissions or a guaranteed draw for the workweek against commissions to be earned within that workweek — must exceed 1.5 times the minimum wage for each hour worked; that this payment must be made in each pay period, so that it is not permissible to defer any part of the wages due for one period until payment of the wages for a later period; that compliance is determined on a workweek basis; and that the second component (more than half of earnings from commissions) must also be satisfied in each workweek, with overtime due for any week in which it is not met, although the agency will defer the actual determination until the reconciliation date after the second pay period. The California Supreme Court in Peabody quoted the first three of these points and adopted the agency's interpretation after independently determining that it was correct. The Manual further states that a guaranteed draw counts toward the earnings prong only if it can be recovered from commissions earned in that same workweek and not from future workweeks; that whether commissions constitute most of the employee's pay is tested over a "representative period" of not less than one month; that the employer bears the responsibility of proving the exemption and must keep records clearly indicating the amount and nature of payments, including a copy or summary of the commission agreement and the applicable representative period; and that consistent commission earnings below, at, or near the draw are indicative of a commission plan that is not bona fide.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 50.6.1 (section 50 pages carry a June 2002 footer; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: 1. In order to comply with the requirements of the exemption and of L.C. § 204, for each workweek in the pay period the earnings of the employee, whether actual commissions or a guaranteed draw for the work week against commissions to be earned within such work week, must exceed 1.5 times the minimum wage for each hour worked during the pay period. 2. As stated above, the payment of the earnings of more than 1.5 times the minimum wage for each hour worked must be made in each pay period. Therefore, it is not permissible to defer any part of the wages due for one period until payment of the wages due for a later period. 3. Compliance with the requirements of the exemption is determined on a workweek basis. The minimum compensation component of the exemption must be satisfied in each workweek and paid in each pay period.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 50.6.1, item 4 (section 50 pages carry a June 2002 footer; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: 4. The second component of the exemption, namely at least 50% of earnings from commissions, must also be satisfied in each workweek. However, the actual determination of compliance can be deferred until the reconciliation date following the end of the second pay period. Overtime will be due for any week in which the second component is not met.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 50.6.4.1 (section 50 pages carry a June 2002 footer; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: To satisfy the exemption, however, for each workweek the employee must be paid a guaranteed draw that exceeds 1.5 times the minimum wage and that can be recovered only from commissions earned in that workweek and not from commissions earned in future workweeks. This is so because every workweek must stand alone for purposes of minimum wage and overtime computation.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §§ 50.6.4.3-50.6.4.4 (section 50 pages carry a June 2002 footer; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: Representative Period. Whether compensation representing commissions constitutes most of an employee’s pay so as to satisfy the exemption must be determined by testing the employee’s compensation for a “representative period” of not less than 1 month.

citations.quote: Consistent commission earnings below, at, or near the draw are indicative of a commission plan that is not bona fide. If the commission plan is found to be invalid, overtime will be due for all weeks in which the exemption was claimed.

citations.quote: we adopt its interpretation having independently determined that it is correct

expectedJSON.gap: The DLSE Manual is an agency enforcement guide, not a regulation; the California Supreme Court has stated that its enforcement policies are not entitled to deference (Peabody, citing Martinez v. Combs), and the Areso court afforded the Manual no deference in construing section 204.1, while Peabody adopted the section 50.6.1 statements quoted here as correct after independent review. The Manual's representative-period position borrows a federal regulation (29 C.F.R. § 779.417) that was not fetched for this document. The pages containing section 50.6 carry a "JUNE, 2002" footer within the Manual as currently posted by the Department of Industrial Relations; other portions of the Manual carry later revision dates. The Manual's section 50.6.4 discussion of advances and draws cites Agnew v. Cameron (1967) 247 Cal.App.2d 619, which was not fetched; draws against commission are addressed in this corpus's separate Wage Advances and Draws Against Commission information sheet.

expectedJSON.body: By its terms, section 3(D) removes only the overtime provisions of subsections 3(A), (B), and (C). It does not exempt the employee from the wage orders' other requirements. In particular, section 4(B) of Wage Order 4-2001 requires every employer to pay each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise — and Peabody's footnote 7 applied the same no-reassignment rule to the minimum wage, observing that the answer is, if anything, clearer in that context. Separately, Labor Code section 2751 requires that whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment for services to be rendered within California and the contemplated method of payment involves commissions, the contract must be in writing and set forth the method by which the commissions are computed and paid; the employer must give the employee a signed copy and obtain a signed receipt. That requirement applies to commission-paid employment regardless of whether the exemption is met. Finally, Wage Orders 4 and 7 each provide that sections 3 through 12 do not apply at all to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities as defined in those orders; the commissioned employee exemption operates within section 3 for employees who are otherwise covered by it.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(B) (California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: (B) Every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise.

citations.case: Peabody v. Time Warner Cable, Inc. (2014) 59 Cal.4th 662, fn. 7 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: wages paid in one pay period cannot be reassigned to satisfy other pay periods’ compensation requirements. If anything, the answer is clearer in the minimum wage context.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2751(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within this state and the contemplated method of payment of the employee involves commissions, the contract shall be in writing and shall set forth the method by which the commissions shall be computed and paid. (b) The employer shall give a signed copy of the contract to every employee who is a party thereto and shall obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 1(A) (California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.quote: (A) Provisions of Sections 3 through 12 shall not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states what the wage orders and Labor Code section 2751 provide and does not catalog every other wage-order obligation (meal and rest periods, records, reporting-time pay, and the like) that continues to apply to a commissioned employee; those subjects are addressed in this corpus's separate information sheets. Section 2751's remedies and its exclusions of certain bonuses and incentive payments from "commission" for its own purposes are addressed in this corpus's Commission Agreement document and are not repeated here. Whether an employee falls within the administrative, executive, or professional exemptions in section 1(A) of the wage orders is governed by the duties and salary tests stated there and in Labor Code section 515(a), which this document does not describe.
